Until now, `script.js` ran from top to bottom and stopped, with two prompts freezing the page along the way. In this lesson the page starts responding to the player instead: a Start button begins a round, and clicking MISAbot scores a point.

## What an event is

An **event** is something that happens on the page: a click, a key press, the mouse moving, a text box changing. You can ask the browser to run a function every time a particular event happens to a particular element. That function is called a **listener**, or an event handler.

<Playground>
```html
<button id="hello">Say hello</button>
```
```js
const button = document.querySelector("#hello");

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("Hello from a click!");
});

console.log("Listening…");
```
</Playground>

`addEventListener` takes two arguments: the name of the event, and the function to run. Press **▶ Run**: `Listening…` appears right away, because the script finishes immediately. Then click the button in the preview a few times. The listener runs once per click, long after the script ended.

<Stepper kind="event" />

That's the mental model from [What is JavaScript?](../../javascript/#your-first-mental-model): the script sets things up, then the page waits and answers events.

## Pass the function, don't call it

You can give `addEventListener` an arrow function, as above, or the name of a function you defined earlier. Either way, you're handing the browser a function to call later.

```js
function sayHello() {
  console.log("Hello!");
}

button.addEventListener("click", sayHello);   // Correct: the browser calls it on each click
button.addEventListener("click", sayHello()); // Wrong: calls it once, right now
```

<Predict question="The page loads, then you click the button twice. What appears in the console?" options={['"Hi!" twice, once per click', '"Hi!" once, before any click', 'Nothing at all']} answer={1}>
```js
function sayHi() {
  console.log("Hi!");
}

button.addEventListener("click", sayHi());
```

The parentheses call `sayHi` immediately, while the listener is being added, so `Hi!` appears once. `sayHi()` returns `undefined`, and that's what gets handed to `addEventListener`, so the clicks do nothing. Removing the parentheses fixes it.
</Predict>

## The event object

When the browser calls your listener, it passes one argument: an **event object** describing what happened. Name the parameter `event` (some code shortens it to `e`).

<Playground>
```html
<button id="like"><img src="assets/misabot.png" alt="" width="48" /> Like</button>
```
```js
const button = document.querySelector("#like");

button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log(event.type);
  console.log(event.target);
  console.log(event.currentTarget);
});
```
</Playground>

Click the picture, then click the word **Like**, and compare the output:

- `event.type` is the name of the event: `"click"`.
- `event.target` is the exact element you clicked. Clicking the picture gives the `<img>`.
- `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running. It's always the button here.

Each hole on our board holds a picture and a label, so a click on MISAbot's face has the `<img>` as its target. We'll use `currentTarget` to get the hole itself.

## Read what the player typed

Text boxes and menus have a `value` property holding the current text or choice:

<Playground>
```html
<input id="nickname" placeholder="Nickname" />
<select id="speed">
  <option value="slow">Slow</option>
  <option value="normal" selected>Normal</option>
  <option value="fast">Fast</option>
</select>
<button id="show">Show</button>
```
```js
const nickname = document.querySelector("#nickname");
const speed = document.querySelector("#speed");
const showButton = document.querySelector("#show");

showButton.addEventListener("click", () => {
  const playerName = nickname.value.trim() || "Player";
  console.log(`${playerName} picked ${speed.value}`);
});
```
</Playground>

Read `value` inside the listener, at the moment of the click. Reading it at the top of the script would only capture the empty box from when the page loaded.

`<select>` gives the `value` attribute of the chosen `<option>`, which is why the options say `value="slow"` and so on.

## Apply it to the game

The prompts go away in this step. A text box, a speed menu, and a Start button replace them, and a score and timer show above the board.

### Update the page

Replace all of `workshop/index.html` with:

```html title="workshop/index.html"
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
    <title>Bop the Bot</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />
  </head>
  <body>
    <main class="game">
      <h1>Bop the Bot</h1>
      <p id="greeting">Type your name, choose a speed, and press Start.</p>

      <fieldset id="controls" class="controls">
        <label>
          Name
          <input id="player-name" type="text" placeholder="Player" maxlength="20" />
        </label>
        <label>
          Speed
          <select id="speed">
            <option value="slow">Slow</option>
            <option value="normal" selected>Normal</option>
            <option value="fast">Fast</option>
          </select>
        </label>
        <button id="start-button" type="button">Start</button>
      </fieldset>

      <div class="stats">
        <p>Score: <strong id="score">0</strong></p>
        <p>Time: <strong id="time">30</strong>s</p>
      </div>

      <div id="board" class="board"></div>
      <p id="message" class="message" role="status"></p>
    </main>

    <script src="script.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>
```

The `<fieldset>` groups the three controls. Disabling a fieldset disables everything inside it, which we'll use to lock the controls during a round. `role="status"` lets screen readers announce the end-of-round message.

### Settings and elements

In `workshop/script.js`, delete `askName`, `askSpeed`, and everything after `hideBot` (the greeting, the demo, and its timers). Keep the board functions.

At the top, after `POP_DELAYS`, add the round length and find the elements the game will update:

```js title="Top of workshop/script.js"
const KEYS = ["q", "w", "e", "a", "s", "d", "z", "x", "c"];
const POP_DELAYS = { slow: 1100, normal: 850, fast: 600 };
const ROUND_SECONDS = 30;

const controls = document.querySelector("#controls");
const nameInput = document.querySelector("#player-name");
const speedSelect = document.querySelector("#speed");
const startButton = document.querySelector("#start-button");
const scoreDisplay = document.querySelector("#score");
const timeDisplay = document.querySelector("#time");
const message = document.querySelector("#message");
```

### A rank for the final score

After `hideBot`, add a function that turns a score into a short title. Each `return` ends the function, so the first matching line wins:

```js title="Add after hideBot"
function rankFor(score) {
  if (score >= 25) {
    return "Legendary bopper";
  }
  if (score >= 15) {
    return "Quick hands";
  }
  if (score >= 5) {
    return "Nice warm-up";
  }
  return "MISAbot got away this time";
}
```

### The state of a round

A game needs to remember things between events: the score, the time left, where MISAbot is, and whether a round is running. Build the board, then make a variable for each piece of **state**:

```js title="Add after rankFor"
const holes = createBoard(document.querySelector("#board"));

let playerName = "Player";
let score = 0;
let misses = 0;
let timeLeft = ROUND_SECONDS;
let currentHole = null;
let isPlaying = false;
let popTimer = null;
let clockTimer = null;

function updateStats() {
  scoreDisplay.textContent = score;
  timeDisplay.textContent = timeLeft;
}

function popUp() {
  if (currentHole !== null) {
    hideBot(currentHole);
  }
  currentHole = randomHole(holes, currentHole);
  showBot(currentHole);
}
```

`popTimer` and `clockTimer` will hold timer ids so we can stop the timers later. `popUp` is the same as before.

### Start, tick, and end a round

```js title="Add after popUp"
function startGame() {
  if (isPlaying) {
    return;
  }
  playerName = nameInput.value.trim() || "Player";
  score = 0;
  misses = 0;
  timeLeft = ROUND_SECONDS;
  isPlaying = true;
  controls.disabled = true;
  message.textContent = `Go, ${playerName}!`;
  updateStats();

  popUp();
  popTimer = setInterval(popUp, POP_DELAYS[speedSelect.value]);
  clockTimer = setInterval(tick, 1000);
}

function tick() {
  timeLeft -= 1;
  updateStats();
  if (timeLeft <= 0) {
    endGame();
  }
}

function endGame() {
  if (!isPlaying) {
    return;
  }
  isPlaying = false;
  clearInterval(popTimer);
  clearInterval(clockTimer);
  if (currentHole !== null) {
    hideBot(currentHole);
    currentHole = null;
  }
  controls.disabled = false;
  message.textContent = `${playerName}, you bopped ${score} bots and missed ${misses}. ${rankFor(score)}!`;
}
```

`startGame` resets everything, reads the name and speed at the moment Start is pressed, and starts two timers: one moves MISAbot, the other counts down once a second. `tick` stops the round at zero. The early `return` lines make both functions safe to call at the wrong time; starting twice won't create extra timers.

### Bop a hole

```js title="Add after endGame"
function bop(hole) {
  if (!isPlaying) {
    return;
  }
  if (hole === currentHole) {
    score += 1;
    hideBot(hole);
    currentHole = null;
    hole.classList.add("bopped");
    setTimeout(() => hole.classList.remove("bopped"), 250);
  } else {
    misses += 1;
  }
  updateStats();
}
```

A bop scores only if MISAbot is in that hole. The `bopped` class flashes the hole for a quarter of a second, then a timer removes it.

### Listen for clicks

Finally, connect the events. Every hole gets a click listener, and so does the Start button:

```js title="Add at the end of workshop/script.js"
function handleHoleClick(event) {
  bop(event.currentTarget);
}

for (const hole of holes) {
  hole.addEventListener("click", handleHoleClick);
}

startButton.addEventListener("click", startGame);
```

`event.currentTarget` is the hole, even when the click landed on MISAbot's picture or the key label inside it.

## Run and check

Type a name, choose a speed, and press **Start**. The timer should count down from 30, and the controls should look faded. Click MISAbot to score; click an empty hole to see a miss counted. When time runs out, MISAbot disappears, the message shows your result, and **Start** works again.

The script now spends almost all its time waiting. Every change on the page comes from a listener or a timer.
